message.content:
The total number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure, often called the *Shannon number*, was first estimated by Claude Shannon in 1950 and has since been refined by computer analysis. It represents an upper bound on the number of unique board configurations that satisfy all of the rules of chess (piece placement, castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.).  

In contrast, the number of possible complete games (sequences of moves from start to finish) is even larger, roughly **10¹²⁰**.
